elements.quote: We conducted meta-analyses, network meta-analyses, and Trial Sequential Analyses (TSA).
elements.reason: The abstract (Methods and Findings) describes methods typical of a systematic review (meta-analyses, network meta-analyses, TSA) and refers to searching for randomized trials, but does not explicitly label the report as a 'systematic review' in the abstract text.

elements.quote: Our objective was to assess the effectiveness and safety of COVID-19 vaccines through analyses of all currently available randomized clinical trials.
elements.reason: The abstract gives a clear statement of the main objective/review question.

elements.quote: We searched the databases CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, and other sources from inception to June 17, 2021 for randomized clinical trials assessing vaccines for COVID-19.
elements.reason: The abstract specifies that randomized clinical trials of COVID-19 vaccines were sought (an inclusion criterion) but does not explicitly state detailed inclusion and exclusion criteria.

elements.quote: We searched the databases CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, and other sources from inception to June 17, 2021 for randomized clinical trials assessing vaccines for COVID-19.
elements.reason: The abstract names the information sources searched and provides the date up to which searches were conducted.

elements.quote: At least two independent reviewers screened studies, extracted data, and assessed risks of bias.
elements.reason: The abstract states that risk of bias was assessed by independent reviewers but does not specify the risk-of-bias tool or detailed methods in the abstract.

elements.quote: We conducted meta-analyses, network meta-analyses, and Trial Sequential Analyses (TSA).
elements.reason: The abstract specifies the analytical and synthesis methods used to present results.

elements.quote: We identified 46 trials; 35 trials randomizing 219 864 participants could be included in our analyses.
elements.reason: The abstract reports the total number of included trials and participants and indicates these were randomized clinical trials (summarizing key study characteristics).

elements.quote: Our meta-analyses showed that mRNA vaccines (efficacy, 95% [95% confidence interval (CI), 92% to 97%]; 71 514 participants; 3 trials; moderate certainty); inactivated vaccines (efficacy, 61% [95% CI, 52% to 68%]; 48 029 participants; 3 trials; moderate certainty); protein subunit vaccines (efficacy, 77% [95% CI, - 5%to 95%]; 17 737 participants; 2 trials; low certainty); and viral vector vaccines (efficacy 68%[95% CI, 61% to 74%]; 71 401 participants; 5 trials; low certainty) prevented COVID19.
elements.reason: The abstract presents results for main outcomes (vaccine efficacy) and provides numbers of trials and participants for each vaccine type.

elements.quote: mRNA vaccines (efficacy, 95% [95% confidence interval (CI), 92% to 97%]; 71 514 participants; 3 trials; moderate certainty)
elements.reason: For conducted meta-analyses, the abstract reports summary estimates with confidence intervals for main outcomes.

elements.quote: All vaccines were more effective than placebo. The two mRNA vaccines ... were likely superior to the remaining vaccines.
elements.reason: The abstract/results text indicates the direction of effect (vaccines more effective than placebo) and which vaccines were favored/superior.

elements.quote: Viral vector vaccines decreased mortality (risk ratio, 0.25 [95% CI 0.09 to 0.67]; 67 563 participants; 3 trials, low certainty), but comparable data on inactivated, mRNA, and protein subunit vaccines were imprecise.
elements.reason: The abstract briefly notes imprecision for some results and reports low/moderate certainty for outcomes, but it does not provide a more comprehensive summary of limitations such as risk of bias, inconsistency, and other limitations in the abstract.

elements.quote: Our meta-analyses showed that mRNA vaccines ... inactivated vaccines ... protein subunit vaccines ... and viral vector vaccines ... prevented COVID19. ... None of the vaccines showed evidence of a difference on serious adverse events, but observational evidence suggested rare serious adverse events. All the vaccines increased the risk of non-serious adverse events.
elements.reason: The abstract provides an overall interpretation of the results and mentions implications regarding adverse events and effectiveness.

elements.quote: Funding: The Copenhagen Trial Unit provided support in the form of salaries for SKK, EvR, FS, SJ, EEN, JF, JJP, JCJ and CG.
elements.reason: The abstract includes the primary source of funding for the review.
The abstract and retrieved abstract-equivalent text do not provide a registration name or registration number.

elements.quote: COVID-19 is caused by Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus 2 (SARS-Cov-2) [1]. Since the observation of the first patients with COVID-19 in Wuhan in 2019, the disease quickly became a global pandemic [2]. As of September 6 th , 2021 more than 221 million individuals developed COVID-19 and 4.6 million died globally [2]. Currently, there are only a few interventions hat seem able to benefit the clinical course of COVID-19 [3]. Therefore, preventive measures are of vital importance to control COVID-19. The scientific, medical, and industrial communities have embarked on efforts to develop safe vaccines [4, 5]. At September 13 th , 2021 about 104 vaccines are being tested in humans, with 33 having reached phase III trials [6]. Of these, five vaccines were abandoned due to either lack of response or an undesirable adverse event (e.g., tested false positive for HIV), eight have been approved for full use, and eleven have been authorized for early or limited use [6]. With the rapid development, approval of vaccines for COVID-19, and the growing number of viral variants, there is a need for systematic reviews critically appraising the topic.
elements.reason: Background and introduction describe the current global burden, the limited interventions, the number/status of vaccine candidates, and note uncertainties (rapid development, variants) establishing current knowledge and uncertainties.

elements.quote: With the rapid development, approval of vaccines for COVID-19, and the growing number of viral variants, there is a need for systematic reviews critically appraising the topic. We recently published the first version of our review as a preprint, showing effects of mRNA and viral vector vaccines [7]. The aim of this second version of our living systematic review is to assess the effectiveness and safety of COVID-19 vaccines through analyses of all currently available randomized clinical trials.
elements.reason: The text explicitly states the need for systematic reviews given rapid vaccine development and variants, and states the aim to assess effectiveness and safety, explaining the importance and need for the review.

elements.quote: We recently published the first version of our review as a preprint, showing effects of mRNA and viral vector vaccines [7]. The aim of this second version of our living systematic review is to assess the effectiveness and safety of COVID-19 vaccines through analyses of all currently available randomized clinical trials.
elements.reason: The authors acknowledge a prior version of their review (cited as a preprint) and state that this is the second version of their living systematic review, thereby explaining the need for this updated review in relation to previous work.
No text in the retrieved evidence describes the proposed mechanism of action of the vaccines; the introduction/background notes vaccine development but does not explain biological mechanisms.

The review concerns standard vaccine interventions rather than complex multi-component delivery contexts; no evidence suggests the review addresses complex interventions or delivery contexts requiring a logic model.

elements.quote: The aim of this second version of our living systematic review is to assess the effectiveness and safety of COVID-19 vaccines through analyses of all currently available randomized clinical trials.
elements.reason: An explicit objective is stated (assessing effectiveness and safety of COVID-19 vaccines in randomized trials), but the statement is not presented using a question-formulation framework (e.g., PICO) as required by the element.

elements.quote: We included randomized clinical trials with any control group, i.e. vaccine versus placebo, 'active placebo', no intervention, another vaccine aiming at preventing COVID-19, or any other 'active' comparator [8].
elements.reason: For an intervention review, the planned comparisons are explicitly stated, specifying interventions (any COVID-19 vaccine), comparators (placebo, active placebo, no intervention, another vaccine, or other active comparator) and inclusion of any participant groups.

elements.quote: We searched for and included randomized clinical trials, irrespective of publication status, year, and language. We included trials with any participant irrespective of prior exposure, age, sex, comorbidities, immune status, and risk group [8]. We included any vaccine aiming to prevent COVID-19 irrespective of dose and duration of administration. We included randomized clinical trials with any control group, i.e. vaccine versus placebo, 'active placebo', no intervention, another vaccine aiming at preventing COVID-19, or any other 'active' comparator [8].
elements.reason: The manuscript specifies key study characteristics used for eligibility: study design (randomized clinical trials), participant characteristics (broadly inclusive), interventions (any COVID-19 vaccine, any dose/duration), and comparators. However, it does not explicitly state settings or any follow-up requirements as eligibility criteria (follow-up durations appear only in Results), so the full set of study-characteristic eligibility items is only partially reported.

elements.quote: We searched for and included randomized clinical trials, irrespective of publication status, year, and language.
elements.reason: The review explicitly states eligibility criteria for report characteristics, declaring inclusion irrespective of publication status, year, and language.
No information is provided distinguishing exclusion because outcomes were not measured from exclusion because outcome results were not reported in the supplied evidence.

elements.quote: All included trials assessed a COVID-19 vaccine compared with placebo (n = 32) or a control vaccine not immunogenic towards COVID-19 (n = 3). The included vaccines were based on mRNA ...; viral vectors ...; protein-subunit ...; or inactivated virus ... (Table 5).
elements.reason: The review specifies the groups used in syntheses (vaccine versus placebo or non-immunogenic control) and categorizes vaccines by type (mRNA, viral vector, protein-subunit, inactivated), linking groupings to the comparisons addressed in the review objectives.

No rationale for any notable restrictions on study eligibility (e.g., restrictions and their justification) is provided in the supplied evidence; only broad inclusions are stated and protocol is referenced.

elements.quote: We searched the databases CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, and other sources from inception to June 17, 2021 for randomized clinical trials assessing vaccines for COVID-19.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly reports the date up to which searches were conducted (June 17, 2021).

elements.quote: We searched the databases CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, and other sources from inception to June 17, 2021 for randomized clinical trials assessing vaccines for COVID-19.
elements.reason: Database names are provided (CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase) and an overall coverage timeframe ('from inception to June 17, 2021') is given, but the search interface/platform for each database and database-specific coverage dates are not reported.
No study registers, regulatory databases, or online repositories searched are named, nor are any date restrictions for such sources reported in the provided evidence.
No websites, search engines, or other online sources with names or URLs are reported in the supplied evidence.
The evidence does not name any organisations or manufacturers that were contacted to identify studies.
No information is provided about types of individuals contacted to identify studies.
The types of reference lists examined (e.g., reference lists of included studies, systematic reviews) are not specified in the provided text.
No details on backward or forward citation searching (seed reports, citation index/platform, search date) are reported in the supplied evidence.
There is no reporting of journals or conference proceedings consulted, their covered dates, or search methods in the provided evidence.

No full search strategies (search strings as run) for each database, register, or website are reported in the provided evidence. The text refers readers to the published protocol or S1 File for details but does not present the complete strategies in the manuscript excerpts supplied.

elements.quote: We searched the databases CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, and other sources from inception to June 17, 2021 for randomized clinical trials assessing vaccines for COVID-19.
elements.reason: The manuscript specifies databases searched and the date range ('from inception to June 17, 2021'), which partially describes limits. However, justification of these limits by reference to the eligibility criteria is not provided in the supplied evidence (although the review states inclusion irrespective of publication status, year, and language elsewhere, no justification tied to eligibility criteria is given).

elements.quote: An experienced information specialist performed weekly literature searches. For details regarding databases, searches, and screening methods see our published protocol [8] or S1 File.
elements.reason: The manuscript cites a published protocol and S1 File for details of searches, which indicates published search approaches are referenced. However, the supplied evidence does not present the published search approaches or filters themselves nor describe any adaptations within the manuscript text shown.
No information is provided in the supplied evidence about use of natural-language processing or text-analysis tools to identify or refine search terms.
No tools used to translate search strings between sources are specified in the provided evidence.
The supplied excerpts contain no description of any validation of the search strategy, validation process, or validation studies.
There is no mention in the provided evidence of any peer review of the search strategy (e.g., PRESS) or description of such a process.

The manuscript excerpts do not state that the search structure was not based on PICO, nor do they describe a final conceptual structure or explorations used to develop the search; no relevant information is provided.

elements.quote: At least two independent reviewers screened studies, extracted data, and assessed risks of bias.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly reports the number of reviewers (at least two) who screened studies and extracted data.

elements.quote: Two authors independently screened and extracted data.
elements.reason: The manuscript states that two authors worked independently for screening and data extraction.
No description found of how screening disagreements were resolved (no mention of consensus procedures, third reviewer, or arbitration).
No information reported on processes to obtain or confirm eligibility information from study investigators.
No methods reported for translating abstracts or full articles for eligibility assessment.
No description of integration of automation tools into the selection process (none reported in text).
No identification or reporting of externally derived classifiers, their version/reference, role, or records removed prior to screening.
No information about internally derived classifiers, their use, training, or validation was reported.
No description found of machine-learning prioritisation tools or any screening stopping/prioritisation rules.
No information reported on use of crowdsourcing platforms or their integration into study selection.
No description of previously screened datasets used to eliminate records or how they were derived.

elements.quote: At least two independent reviewers screened studies, extracted data, and assessed risks of bias.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly reports the number of reviewers (at least two) who extracted data from reports.

elements.quote: Two authors independently screened and extracted data.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly states that two authors worked independently for screening and data extraction.
No text in the provided evidence describes processes used to resolve disagreements between data collectors.
No information in the retrieved evidence describes processes for obtaining or confirming data from study investigators.
No information in the retrieved evidence describes use, training, or validation of any automation tools for data collection.
No information in the retrieved evidence reports methods used to translate articles for data collection.
No information in the retrieved evidence specifies software used to extract data from figures.
No information in the retrieved evidence describes decision rules for selecting data from multiple reports or resolving inconsistencies.

elements.quote: Our primary outcomes were allcause mortality; vaccine efficacy defined by either preventing COVID-19 symptoms plus positive polymerase chain rection (PCR) test, preventing severe COVID-19 symptoms plus positive PCR test, or preventing positive PCR test only; and serious adverse events [10]. Our secondary outcomes were health-related quality of life and adverse events not considered serious [8].
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly lists primary and secondary outcome domains and defines vaccine efficacy by specific measurement definitions (symptoms + PCR, severe symptoms + PCR, or PCR only).

elements.quote: We used the trial results reported at maximum follow-up for all outcomes.
elements.reason: The time frame for measurement is specified as the trial-reported maximum follow-up; additional support in text_10 gives the median follow-up range (35 to 92 days).

elements.quote: We used the trial results reported at maximum follow-up for all outcomes. We used intention-to-treat data if provided by the trialists [8].
elements.reason: The authors state their approach to which results were sought (selecting trial results at maximum follow-up and using intention-to-treat data when provided), thereby stating whether all compatible results were sought and the principle used.

elements.quote: We used the trial results reported at maximum follow-up for all outcomes. We used intention-to-treat data if provided by the trialists [8].
elements.reason: When not all possible time points/analyses were used, the process to select results is described (choose the trial-reported maximum follow-up and use intention-to-treat data when available).
No information in the provided evidence about any changes to outcome-domain inclusion, definitions, or importance or rationales for such changes.
No information in the provided evidence about any changes to the processes for selecting results within eligible outcome domains or rationales for such changes.

elements.quote: Our primary outcomes were allcause mortality; vaccine efficacy defined by either preventing COVID-19 symptoms plus positive polymerase chain rection (PCR) test, preventing severe COVID-19 symptoms plus positive PCR test, or preventing positive PCR test only; and serious adverse events [10].
elements.reason: The authors report which outcomes are primary (i.e. those most important) but do not provide an explicit rationale for why these outcomes were prioritised in the provided evidence.

elements.quote: Our primary outcomes were allcause mortality; vaccine efficacy defined by either preventing COVID-19 symptoms plus positive polymerase chain rection (PCR) test, preventing severe COVID-19 symptoms plus positive PCR test, or preventing positive PCR test only; and serious adverse events [10]. Our secondary outcomes were health-related quality of life and adverse events not considered serious [8]. We used the trial results reported at maximum follow-up for all outcomes. We used intention-to-treat data if provided by the trialists [8]. Several exploratory outcomes were predefined in our protocol and will be presented in a subsequent publication [8].
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly lists and defines primary and secondary outcomes and mentions exploratory outcomes and use of intention-to-treat and maximum follow-up; however, it does not comprehensively list or define other variables (e.g. full participant characteristics, funding sources) sought across studies—though some trial characteristics are presented elsewhere (see table_5). Therefore reporting is partial.

elements.quote: To assess the potential impact of missing data, we performed sensitivity analyses using 'best-worst' and 'worst-best' analysis [8, 15]. We used intention-to-treat data if provided by the trialists [8].
elements.reason: The authors describe methods to address missing outcome data (sensitivity analyses and preference for intention-to-treat data), indicating some assumptions/approaches to missing information; however, there is no detailed description of specific assumptions made about other missing or unclear study information (e.g. how unclear participant or intervention data were handled), so the requirement is only partly met.

elements.quote: This systematic review with meta-analyses was conducted in accordance with the reporting guideline provided in the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta- Analysis (PRISMA) statement [9, 10]. This review was carried out following recommendations outlined in the Cochrane Handbook of Systematic Reviews of Interventions [11]. More details on our methods can be found in our published protocol [8, 12].
elements.reason: The manuscript cites the PRISMA reporting guideline, the Cochrane Handbook, and the published protocol as the sources guiding methods and data collection, satisfying the conditional requirement to cite the tool(s) used to determine which data items to collect.

elements.quote: Risk of bias assessment. Our risk of bias assessment was based on the Cochrane risk of bias tool version 2 (RoB 2) [13].
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly names the risk-of-bias tool and its version (Cochrane RoB 2).
No text in the provided evidence specifies the domains, components, or individual items assessed by the RoB 2 tool.

elements.quote: Ten trials were at overall low risk of bias [43, 47, 48, 67], seventeen trials were at overall some concerns [34, 36, 38, 39, 41, 42, 46, 51-53], and eight trials were at overall high risk of bias (S1 File) [37, 40, 45].
elements.reason: The manuscript reports overall risk-of-bias judgments for included trials (low, some concerns, high), but it does not provide the rules or criteria used to derive those overall judgements in the provided evidence.
No information in the retrieved evidence describes any adaptations made to an existing risk-of-bias tool.
There is no indication in the evidence that a newly developed risk-of-bias tool was created; the authors report using RoB 2, so this item does not apply.

elements.quote: At least two independent reviewers screened studies, extracted data, and assessed risks of bias.
elements.reason: The manuscript states that at least two independent reviewers assessed risk of bias, indicating number and independence, but the retrieved evidence does not report procedures for resolving disagreements.
No description in the provided evidence of processes used to obtain or confirm risk-of-bias information from study investigators.
The retrieved evidence does not describe use of any automation tools for risk-of-bias assessment (no use, training, performance, or validation details reported).

elements.quote: Association measures. Wecalculated risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence interval (CI).
elements.reason: The methods section explicitly states the effect measure used (risk ratios with 95% CIs) for the analyses.

elements.quote: DARIS: 1 350 077 (Pc 0.03%; RRR 20%; alpha 1.67%; beta 10%; diversity 0%)
elements.reason: Tables and DARIS notes report an assumed relative risk reduction (RRR 20%) and related thresholds used in Trial Sequential Analysis, which are thresholds applied to interpret effect size in the TSA.

elements.quote: · The basis for the assumed risk (e.g., the median control group risk across studies) is provided in footnotes. The corresponding risk (and its 95% confidence interval) is based on the assumed risk in the comparison group and the relative effect of the intervention (and its 95% CI).
elements.reason: The manuscript describes how relative effects (RRs) are converted into corresponding absolute risks using an assumed control-group risk, indicating the method used to re-express synthesized relative results as absolute risks.
No text in the provided evidence justifies why risk ratios were chosen as the effect measure (no explicit rationale for choice of effect measure is reported).

elements.quote: 46 trials met our inclusion criteria [34-65], of which 35 trials [34, 36-42, 44-50, 53-59, 61-65] randomizing 219 864 participants provided data for our predefined meta-analyses.
elements.reason: The manuscript reports overall inclusion criteria and explicitly states how many trials provided data for the predefined meta-analyses (text_10). The methods also state broad inclusion criteria for trials (text_8: "We searched for and included randomized clinical trials... We included any vaccine... We included randomized clinical trials with any control group") and the tables (table_4/table_5) tabulate trials by vaccine type, indicating grouping by intervention class. However, the paper does not explicitly describe the detailed processes used to decide which specific studies were eligible for each individual synthesis (for example, a step-by-step decision rule or explicit comparison of study intervention characteristics against planned groups for each synthesis). Therefore the requirement is only partially satisfied.

elements.quote: We used the trial results reported at maximum follow-up for all outcomes. We used intention-to-treat data if provided by the trialists [8]. ... We calculated risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence interval (CI). ... We assessed three primary outcomes and two secondary outcomes. We, therefore, considered a p value of 0.0167 or less as the threshold for statistical significance to adjust for multiplicity [8, 15]. We performed Trial Sequential Analysis on all outcomes, to calculate the diversity-adjusted required information size (DARIS) and the cumulative Z-curve's breach of relevant trial sequential monitoring boundaries [21-23]. ... To assess the potential impact of missing data, we performed sensitivity analyses using 'best-worst' and 'worst-best' analysis [8, 15].
elements.reason: The manuscript reports several procedures for preparing data for synthesis (use of maximum follow-up results, use of intention-to-treat data when provided, calculation of RRs, choice of effect models, multiplicity adjustment, use of Trial Sequential Analysis, and sensitivity analyses to assess impact of missing data). However, it does not fully describe specifics of other data-preparation steps (e.g., detailed handling/conversion of missing summary statistics, imputation rules, or specific data conversions), so the reporting is partial.

elements.quote: Wecreated summary of findings tables including each of the prespecified outcomes (all-cause mortality, vaccine efficacy, serious adverse events, health-related quality of life, and non-serious adverse events) (Tables 1-4).
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly states that summary of findings tables were created and refers to Tables 1-4, indicating the tabular structures used to display results and the data included.

elements.quote: We used forest plots to illustrate summary effect sizes of the comparative effectiveness among interventions.
elements.reason: The methods explicitly state use of forest plots to display meta-analysis results; the results section includes visual figures (forest plots and rank heat plot) supporting use of graphical displays.

elements.quote: Weperformed subgroup analysis assessing different types of vaccines; trials at low compared with at high risk of bias; and trials without against with vested interests.
elements.reason: The manuscript reports subgroup analyses by vaccine type and risk of bias (which implies grouping of studies by these characteristics), but it does not clearly or explicitly describe the specific basis used to order or group studies within individual tables or graphs (e.g., exact ordering rules in tables/figures).
No rationale is provided in the retrieved evidence for using non-standard graphs (e.g., rank heat plot); the manuscript does not explain why non-standard graphical formats were chosen.

elements.quote: We used Stata version 16.1 to analyse data using the metan command for metaanalysis and network suite of commands for network meta-analysis [16-18].
elements.reason: Software (Stata) and version (16.1) plus commands/packages used (metan and network suite) are explicitly reported.

elements.quote: Our review also has limitations. Most of the larger phase III trials presented only interim analyses. The follow-up ranged from only 35 to 92 days.
